cards.title: Use SameSite cookies to block cross-site state-changing requests
cards.summary: SameSite cookie attributes stop another origin from triggering requests that carry a logged-in customer's cookies, defending against cross-site request forgery.
cards.use_when: Configuring session cookies for customer login, cart, or admin accounts, or reviewing whether an authenticated action (e.g. cart change, address update, admin mutation) can be triggered from a third-party page.

cards.title: Recognize IDN homograph attacks against lookalike domains
cards.summary: Unicode look-alike characters let an attacker register a domain that renders identically to a brand domain, so verify the true host and prefer password managers on high-risk flows.
cards.use_when: Training support teams, reviewing brand-domain monitoring, or designing login and admin flows where a customer or staff member might be steered to a lookalike domain via a link in a chat, ad, or email.

cards.title: Be skeptical of HTTPS padlock and EV badges as trust signals
cards.summary: A padlock proves encrypted transport to some server, not that the operator is legitimate, and attackers can obtain certificates freely.
cards.use_when: Deciding which trust indicators to display on a storefront or checkout, or explaining to customers and staff why a padlock is not a legitimacy guarantee.

cards.title: Defend against clickjacking that overlays fake trusted UI
cards.summary: Attackers can hide or overlay interfaces so store actions (buttons, consent, downloads) get clicked under a misleading visual, and the durable defense is framing/isolation control on your own pages.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether your checkout, login, admin, or consent pages can be embedded by third parties, and hardening framing headers for sensitive store surfaces.

cards.title: Manipulated browser history and UI-suppression tricks are perception attacks
cards.summary: Attackers can add embarrassing or misleading entries to a visitor's history and hide the browser UI on scroll, so trust decisions should not rest on ambient browser chrome.
cards.use_when: Assessing how a visitor could be convinced a phishing page is a trusted store (e.g. a fake bank or brand login reached from an ad, chat link, or QR code) and choosing defenses that do not rely on browser chrome.

cards.title: Verify what your URL bar actually shows before trusting subdomains
cards.summary: Browsers render long attacker-controlled subdomains inconsistently, and shrinking the window can hide which domain is real, so teach customers and staff the registrable-domain rule.
cards.use_when: Writing security education for staff or customers, and evaluating whether a URL in a support ticket, ad, or partner link is a real brand domain versus a lookalike subdomain.

cards.title: Treat browser UI/API features as a security-vs-capability tradeoff with fingerprinting cost
cards.summary: Powerful browser APIs enable richer shops but expand attack surface and fingerprinting vectors, and the cost/benefit is judged by how often disabling a feature breaks real sites versus how often it is implicated in exploits.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add a browser-capability-dependent storefront or checkout feature (device APIs, media capture, sandbox/iframe isolation requirements) and judging the customer-risk tradeoff.

cards.title: Check URLs against a safe-browsing list without leaking full browsing history
cards.summary: Safe-browsing style protection queries a reputation list using hash prefixes downloaded locally, so a store or browser can warn on known-bad URLs without sending each full URL to the provider.
cards.use_when: Evaluating or implementing URL reputation/abuse-warning tooling for a storefront, link shortener, or marketplace, and deciding between real-time URL submission and a downloaded prefix list.

cards.title: Design browser security around an assumed-sketchy-site layer
cards.summary: Rather than handicapping the browser with endless prompts, assume users will reach malicious sites and add a separate reputation/warning layer that protects them there.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much friction to add to storefront security prompts (login, payment, download, permission requests) and where to invest instead.

cards.title: Scope untrusted content and tool output as data, not authority
cards.summary: Pages, documents, and agent/tool output can be attacker-influenced and must not be treated as authorization for privileged store actions.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing ecommerce automation (order bots, support agents, listing tools, integrations) that reads external content or tool output and can take store actions.

cards.title: Convert an embarrassing-history or fake-UI trick into a customer-protection test
cards.summary: Use the source's demonstrated browser-abuse techniques as vulnerability conditions to test your own store's exposure rather than as offensive recipes.
cards.use_when: Running a defensive review of storefront pages, popups, and iframes that could be repurposed by an attacker, or training support staff to recognize manipulated browser UI.

cards.title: Use Safe Browsing hash-prefix lookups to block malware/phishing destinations
cards.summary: How browser-style local hash-prefix matching lets you flag malicious URLs without sending full URLs to a third party, and its limits.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to screen outbound links, user-submitted content or redirect URLs (e.g. affiliate links, UGC product listings) against known malicious destinations without leaking every URL to a reputation service.

cards.title: Why hashing is used for integrity and lookup, and what its properties guarantee
cards.summary: The five properties of cryptographic hash functions that make them useful for URL reputation, integrity checks and lookups.
cards.use_when: Choosing or reviewing a hashing scheme for things like URL/entity reputation lists, file-integrity checks on uploaded assets, or tokenizing customer data for lookups.

cards.title: Model side channels on your storefront: a correct system can still leak data
cards.summary: Side-channel attacks reveal information through timing, size or sensor differences even when no code bug exists, which matters for how much you expose cross-site.
cards.use_when: Threat-modeling your storefront or admin pages for what a third-party script or an embedded attacker page could infer about logged-in customers, cart state or history.

cards.title: Fix visited-link and history leaks: browser whitelists, timing and lying APIs
cards.summary: How browsers mitigated CSS-based browsing-history leaks and why the fix is intentionally incomplete, with lessons for styling untrusted links.
cards.use_when: Handling links to third-party or user-submitted destinations on product pages and deciding which link styling is safe to let influence layout or resource loading.

cards.title: Prevent cross-origin state leaks via embedded images and layouts
cards.summary: Images embedded from another origin attach that origin's cookies and can reveal logged-in state through size or layout differences.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing any partner widgets, tracking pixels or third-party scripts that embed requests to your logged-in domains on a storefront or admin panel.

cards.title: Decide how to handle ambient-light and sensor APIs on your storefront
cards.summary: Sensor APIs (ambient light, gyroscope) can leak information through measurable screen or device changes, which shaped whether browsers expose them.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to use device-sensor APIs (light, motion, orientation) in responsive storefront features and how to bound the risk of the data they expose.

cards.title: Prevent command injection in server-side features like file or report generators
cards.summary: Never concatenate untrusted request data into shell commands; use argument-array process APIs that escape inputs.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing any server-side feature that shells out — file viewers, image converters, PDF/CSV exporters, backup scripts — triggered by storefront or admin input.

cards.title: Recognize code injection as the parent category behind XSS and similar bugs
cards.summary: Code injection mixes untrusted user data with interpreter code so the interpreter misreads data as commands.
cards.use_when: Reviewing how any user-supplied value reaches an interpreter (HTML, SQL, shell, template) on your storefront, checkout or admin tooling.

cards.title: Prevent command injection with argument arrays, not string templates
cards.summary: Use language APIs that accept a program plus an argument list so escaping is handled by the runtime, and never build shell strings from user input.
cards.use_when: You are building storefront features that shell out to a tool — image resizing, PDF generation, label printing, inventory export scripts, or any admin automation that runs a program on user-supplied values.

cards.title: Recognize and close SQL injection in store login and lookup queries
cards.summary: Any query that concatenates user input into SQL can be manipulated to bypass login, enumerate the customer table, or delete data — parameterize queries and constrain what the query is allowed to return.
cards.use_when: You are reviewing or building store account login, order lookup, coupon validation, search filters, inventory reports or any admin query that embeds form input or URL parameters into SQL.

cards.title: Understand and bound blind SQL injection as an operational risk
cards.summary: When an injection point does not echo query output, an attacker can still extract data by asking true/false questions through error behavior or response timing, so detection must not depend on visible output.
cards.use_when: You are assessing the risk profile of a store search, filter, order-status lookup or API endpoint that returns a generic success/failure response, and deciding how much effort detection and parameterization deserve.

cards.title: Layer safe-browsing-style URL reputation using local hash prefixes
cards.summary: Download a locally cached list of hash prefixes for known-malicious URLs so most checks happen offline, then confirm only on prefix matches to limit what you disclose.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating or implementing a link-safety or phishing-warning feature for a storefront — for example scanning user-submitted review links, affiliate URLs, supplier links or outbound links in marketing content before they are shown or clicked.

cards.title: Understand side-channel leakage as a class of risk to storefront logic
cards.summary: A system can behave exactly as designed and still leak secrets through timing, power or visual emissions, so security review must consider what observable differences reveal about hidden state.
cards.use_when: You are designing storefront or API logic that must not reveal whether a customer, coupon, account or inventory condition is true — for example email-enumeration checks in password reset, coupon validity endpoints, or stock lookups on a product page.

cards.title: Browser history disclosure via CSS :visited and the whitelist trade-off
cards.summary: Links styled by :visited once let any page read a visitor's browsing history, and the durable fix is restricting which CSS properties can apply to visited links rather than trying to hide the difference.
cards.use_when: You are reviewing a storefront's CSS or third-party scripts embedded on PDP, checkout or content pages, and deciding whether any styling rule could reveal a visitor's prior browsing behavior to that page.

cards.title: Secure handling of retrieved documents and tool output in agent workflows
cards.summary: Text fetched from the web, uploaded by users, or returned by a tool is untrusted data and must never be treated as authorization to change an agent's targets or expand its permissions.
cards.use_when: You are deploying an ecommerce automation agent that reads supplier pages, review content, uploaded CSVs, order notes or API responses and then acts — for example updating prices, drafting replies, creating orders or running scripts.

cards.title: Visited-Link History Leaks and Storefront Fingerprinting Risk
cards.summary: Browsers mitigate visited-link sniffing with CSS whitelists, timing equalization and style lying, but rendering-timing side channels still leak which URLs a user has visited.
cards.use_when: Auditing storefront or marketing-site third-party scripts and ad pixels for the risk that they fingerprint visitors' browsing history, or advising engineering on what a page's own rendering performance reveals about customer behavior.

cards.title: Cross-Site Image Requests and Cookie-Bearing Side Channels
cards.summary: Images embedded on any site send the target origin's cookies automatically, so an attacker can infer login state or read sensitive images via layout and rendering side channels.
cards.use_when: Reviewing cookie attributes, third-party image embeds and account-state endpoints on a storefront, or threat-modeling how a competitor or attacker page could learn whether a customer is logged into your store or payment/email accounts.

cards.title: Ambient-Light Sensor as a Browser-History and Image-Reading Side Channel
cards.summary: An unpermissioned ambient-light API can be abused to infer visited links and even read sensitive images pixel-by-pixel by correlating screen output with room brightness.
cards.use_when: Deciding which browser sensor/permission APIs to allow or request on a storefront or PWA, or assessing privacy exposure of device-sensor features used for theming, games or interactive PDP experiences.

cards.title: Gyroscope API Eavesdropping and Sensor Permission Tradeoffs
cards.summary: Highly precise, unpermissioned motion sensors can pick up acoustic signals and infer speech, illustrating why sensor APIs belong behind permission prompts.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a storefront, web game or interactive product experience should request motion/orientation sensor access, and auditing which sensitive device-permission APIs your site invokes.

cards.title: Why Side Channels and Phishing Resist Full Mitigation
cards.summary: Side channels are pervasive and hard to eliminate, phishing is fundamentally a human problem, and browser security controls always trade off against web capabilities.
cards.use_when: Setting realistic security expectations for a storefront — deciding how much engineering effort to spend on browser-level hardening versus user education, monitoring and account controls.

cards.title: Command Injection in Store Backends and the Argument-Array Fix
cards.summary: Combining untrusted user input into a shell command string lets attackers run OS commands on the server; use argument-array APIs that escape input instead of string concatenation.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or writing any store backend code or admin/integration feature that shells out — file viewers, image/asset processing, export tools, report generators or third-party CLI wrappers.

cards.title: Review store database queries for SQL injection
cards.summary: Find data/code mixing in login, order lookup and catalog queries and replace it with parameter binding.
cards.use_when: Reviewing authentication, search or account-lookup endpoints on a store for SQL injection, or testing whether an input field safely parameterizes queries.

cards.title: Stacked SQL Injection via APIs That Allow Multiple Statements
cards.summary: Some database APIs permit multiple semicolon-separated statements, letting an attacker with an injection point run additional queries such as changing passwords or dropping tables.
cards.use_when: Choosing database query APIs for a store backend and reviewing existing endpoints that run SQL for login, logging or admin operations.

cards.title: Recognize blind SQL injection signals without exposing customer data
cards.summary: Response and timing differences can reveal unsafe queries even when the application hides database output.
cards.use_when: Assessing whether a store endpoint that accepts search/filter input and gives only success/failure or timing feedback could leak database contents, and prioritizing remediation for such endpoints.

cards.title: HSTS: force browsers to HTTPS and rewrite HTTP requests
cards.summary: Deploy Strict-Transport-Security so browsers internally upgrade HTTP requests to HTTPS and block certificate-error bypass for your store domain.
cards.use_when: You are hardening checkout, login and account pages against network interception, and deciding an HSTS rollout plan for your storefront domain.

cards.title: Recognize HSTS as a persistent third-party tracking vector
cards.summary: An ad-network script can set and read HSTS state across subdomains to build a supercookie that survives normal cookie clearing.
cards.use_when: You are assessing third-party scripts, pixels or ad-network embeds on product and checkout pages for privacy and tracking exposure, or responding to a data-subject request to clear tracking state.

cards.title: Treat HTTPS as baseline, not a proof of trustworthiness
cards.summary: HTTPS provides confidentiality, integrity and server authentication, but only as strong as the certificate chain behind it, so it must not be treated as a standalone safety guarantee.
cards.use_when: You are deciding what security claims to make on your storefront landing page or checkout (badges, trust copy) and which protections to actually implement.

cards.title: Use CAA DNS records to constrain who may issue certificates for your domain
cards.summary: Certificate Authority Authorization is an advisory DNS record that tells CAs which issuers are allowed for your domain, reducing rogue issuance without the unreliability of key pinning.
cards.use_when: You are setting up or reviewing domain-level certificate management for your storefront and want an implementable control against mis-issuance.

cards.title: Treat browser certificate pinning as deprecated and use the alternatives
cards.summary: Dynamic public-key pinning (HPKP) was removed from Chrome because chain-building differences, unrecoverable errors and hostile-pinning risk made it too unreliable; CAA, static pinning and certificate transparency replace it for most needs.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating whether to implement HPKP or certificate pinning on your storefront or deciding how to respond to pinning advice from a vendor or agency.

cards.title: Plan HSTS preload carefully: it fixes the first-visit gap but is slow to reverse
cards.summary: Preload lists bake HSTS opt-in into browsers so the first visit is protected, but removal requires waiting on release cycles and getting off the list is difficult.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to submit your storefront domain to the HSTS preload list and how to sequence that decision.

cards.title: Track your HTTPS/HSTS adoption as a migration metric
cards.summary: Migration of a store from HTTP to HTTPS should be run as a measured rollout, not a one-step switch, using max-age ramps and breakage data.
cards.use_when: You are migrating a legacy or large storefront to HTTPS/HSTS and need to sequence the rollout without breaking customers.

cards.title: Harden mixed content by eliminating HTTP subresources on HTTPS pages
cards.summary: Removing HTTP subresources from HTTPS pages closes a class of tampering and tracking exposure, at the cost of breaking pages that still rely on them.
cards.use_when: You are auditing product, category and checkout templates for insecure subresource loads (images, scripts, fonts, pixels) and planning remediation.

cards.title: Do not trust positive security indicators or geographic CA blocking
cards.summary: Lock icons and region-based blocking are unreliable defenses; the source argues both fail in practice and should not be the basis of a storefront security plan.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how to communicate security to shoppers or being asked to approve a 'block by country/region' style control for your store or infrastructure.

cards.title: Keep authentication, authorization, encryption, hashing and signing distinct in store design
cards.summary: Confusing encryption, hashing, signing and authentication leads to wrong security controls; each addresses a different property and the source's TLS discussion illustrates the distinction.
cards.use_when: You are specifying security requirements for storefront accounts, payment integrations, agent credentials or admin access and need to state each control precisely.

cards.title: Treat agents' retrieved documents and tool output as untrusted data
cards.summary: In an agentic storefront workflow, inbound documents, pages and tool responses are data to be evaluated, not authorization for actions.
cards.use_when: You are building or reviewing an ecommerce agent that reads supplier documents, product feeds, customer messages or web pages and can then call tools like price updates, refunds or order changes.

cards.title: Bound validation of storefront attacks to systems you own
cards.summary: When verifying that a vulnerability actually affects your store, test only against your own properties and describe the vulnerability condition rather than weaponizing it.
cards.use_when: You are validating a suspected weakness (timing side channel, credential stuffing, insecure subresource, injection) in your own storefront before remediation.

cards.title: Assume any certificate authority can issue for your store domain
cards.summary: The web PKI lets any CA issue for any domain, so planning must assume impersonation is possible and rely on detection and authorization controls.
cards.use_when: You are threat-modeling domain impersonation of your storefront (phishing clones, fake checkout pages) and choosing which certificate controls to deploy.

cards.title: Expect migration resistance and budget for it
cards.summary: Security migrations provoke strong resistance from some operators; plan ramp, measurement and deprecation rather than arguing about old costs.
cards.use_when: You are pushing an HTTPS/HSTS or mixed-content cleanup across a large store or multi-brand ecommerce organization with legacy systems.

cards.title: Decide between CA-permissive convenience and stricter issuance assurance
cards.summary: There is no reliable way to validate an arbitrary CA's authority; controls must either reduce which CAs can issue for you or detect their failures.
cards.use_when: You are selecting a certificate-issuance strategy or vendor for your store and weighing convenience against assurance.

cards.title: Certificate Transparency: Detection, Not Prevention, for Storefront TLS
cards.summary: CT makes mis-issued TLS certificates publicly discoverable rather than blocking them, so ecommerce operators should monitor logs for their own domains instead of treating CT as attack prevention.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to monitor for fraudulent or mistakenly issued TLS certificates on your store's customer-facing domains.

cards.title: Authentication vs Authorization: Keep Session Tokens Out of the Permission Business
cards.summary: Authentication verifies identity while authorization decides permissions; store session IDs that map to server-side authorization checks rather than embedding permissions in client tokens.
cards.use_when: Designing login, session, and admin-role handling for a storefront or its backend (customer accounts, staff/admin panels).

cards.title: Username Handling Rules: Case-Insensitive Uniqueness, Preserved Display Case
cards.summary: Store usernames case-insensitively with enforced uniqueness while preserving the user's preferred capitalization for display, to avoid duplicate accounts and impersonation collisions.
cards.use_when: Implementing customer account creation and login for a storefront where usernames or display handles are used.

cards.title: Modern Password Policy: Length Over Complexity, Breach-List Checks, No Forced Rotation
cards.summary: The source's updated password guidance is to allow long passwords, enforce a minimum length, drop complexity/rotation rules, and screen new passwords against known breach data.
cards.use_when: Setting password rules for your store's customer accounts or admin logins.

cards.title: Password Handling Mistakes That Break Security and Usability
cards.summary: A catalog of password anti-patterns the source flags — silent truncation, blocked paste, weak hints, on-screen keyboards, and max-length caps — that weaken real security while annoying users.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a login/signup implementation before launch or when auditing an existing storefront's authentication.

cards.title: Defending Against Network-Based Guessing: Rate Limiting, Lockouts, CAPTCHA
cards.summary: Brute force, credential stuffing, and password spraying are distinct online guessing attacks; the source's defenses are rate limiting by username and IP, delays/rejections, and CAPTCHA as a human check.
cards.use_when: Hardening the login endpoint of a storefront or admin panel against automated credential guessing.

cards.title: CAPTCHA Limits: Why Human Checks Alone Won't Stop Bots
cards.summary: The source shows text CAPTCHAs were broken by automated solvers and that relay/outsourcing services and solver APIs defeat CAPTCHAs, so treat them as friction, not proof of humanity.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to rely on CAPTCHA to protect signup, login, or high-abuse store actions (e.g., promo-code redemption, inventory hoarding).

cards.title: Offline Cracking Realities Shape Password-Length Guidance
cards.summary: Password strength should be judged against three attack scenarios — online guessing (slow, network-bound) and offline cracking on a single machine or GPU array (fast) — which is why the source pushes for longer passwords.
cards.use_when: Choosing minimum password length and hash settings for customer or admin accounts based on how exposed your credential database is.

cards.title: Multi-Factor Authentication: Knows, Has, Is — and Why Biometrics Stay on Device
cards.summary: Authentication factors fall into something you know, have, or are; combining factors raises assurance, and biometric data should be handled to avoid the 'can't reset a fingerprint' problem.
cards.use_when: Deciding which authentication factors to offer for customer logins and which to require for admin/staff or high-value store actions (e.g., payouts, price changes).

cards.title: Fake Security Indicators: Anti-Phishing Images and Positive UI Cues Don't Work
cards.summary: Security images and other positive UI indicators are ignored or easily spoofed, so don't build phishing defense on customer-visible badges that attackers can replicate.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether any trust badge, security image, or pre-login indicator on your storefront actually protects customers from phishing lookalikes.

cards.title: Security-vs-Usability Tradeoffs: Match Friction to the Value at Risk
cards.summary: Password and authentication rules are balances between usability and security, so calibrate strictness to the sensitivity of the account rather than applying one policy everywhere.
cards.use_when: Deciding how strict login policy should be for different account tiers in a store (casual shopper accounts vs. accounts with stored payment, payout, or admin access).

cards.title: Defense-in-Depth: Assume the Password Is Already Compromised
cards.summary: The source frames authentication design around building systems that stay secure even when an attacker holds the user's password, using layers rather than a single strong credential.
cards.use_when: Architecting login and account protection for a storefront where credentials commonly leak or get reused across sites.

cards.title: CAPTCHA strength is weaker than it looks — treat it as a speed bump
cards.summary: Published attack research showed solver accuracy against major CAPTCHA schemes ran far above the 1% 'broken' threshold, so CAPTCHA alone cannot be your bot defense.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to rely on CAPTCHA/reCAPTCHA to protect storefront login, account creation, checkout, or admin actions.

cards.title: Reputation scoring and invisible challenges (modern reCAPTCHA-style)
cards.summary: Modern bot defense scores trust from behavior, session and IP reputation across many sites rather than from a visible puzzle, and increasingly runs with no UI at all.
cards.use_when: Choosing or configuring a bot-mitigation service for login, account creation, checkout, or coupon/inventory abuse on your storefront.

cards.title: Step-up re-authentication for sensitive ecommerce actions (sudo mode)
cards.summary: Require the user to re-enter their password before a small set of high-impact account, payment, or address changes, as a defense-in-depth measure analogous to GitHub's sudo mode.
cards.use_when: Designing the admin/customer account flows where you allow changes to saved payment methods, shipping addresses, email/password, or payout/account details.

cards.title: Generic error messages to stop account enumeration on login, signup, and reset
cards.summary: Response discrepancies in login, password-reset, and signup flows let attackers learn which emails/accounts exist, so respond identically regardless of the underlying state.
cards.use_when: Writing the copy, logic, and status codes for storefront login, signup, guest-checkout account detection, and password-reset forms.

cards.title: Avoid timing side channels in authentication code paths
cards.summary: Early returns and skipped work in login handlers create measurable timing differences that reveal whether a user exists, so make both paths do equal work.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or writing login/password-check code where a database or service call only happens when the user exists.

cards.title: Rate limiting authentication attempts — and the shared-IP caveat
cards.summary: Rate limit login and account-recovery attempts so credential stuffing and account enumeration can't be done at scale, while setting limits high enough for shared corporate/NAT IPs.
cards.use_when: Setting thresholds and locking policies for storefront login, password reset, and signup endpoints.

cards.title: Check signup passwords against breach lists (Have I Been Pwned)
cards.summary: Because leaked-password corpora are public, reject/flag passwords your customers choose that appear in known breaches, and alert users whose credentials later surface.
cards.use_when: Choosing and enforcing password policy at account creation and password change on your storefront.

cards.title: Proactively lock or flag accounts after a breach you're tangentially involved with
cards.summary: If you learn a customer's credential is in a breach (yours or another service's), proactively force a reset or lock rather than waiting for stuffing to succeed.
cards.use_when: Incident response and ongoing account hygiene for a storefront whose customers reuse passwords across sites.

cards.title: Store passwords with a maintained adaptive password hasher
cards.summary: Use purpose-built password hashing with unique salts and tested cost settings rather than raw fast hashes or reversible encryption.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing how your storefront stores customer and admin credentials.

cards.title: Why strong passwords alone fail — and what they actually protect
cards.summary: A strong password only blocks guessing and brute force; it does nothing against credential stuffing, phishing, MITM, or a malware-logged keystroke, so treat the password as one layer among several.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to require MFA on your storefront and explaining the value to stakeholders.

cards.title: Use risk-based step-up checks without weakening admin authentication
cards.summary: Use contextual signals to adjust customer authentication while maintaining stronger requirements for privileged actions.
cards.use_when: Designing when to add an MFA prompt in storefront login and account flows without hurting conversion.

cards.title: TOTP: implementing a two-factor second factor without SMS
cards.summary: Time-based one-time passwords authenticate a user by having the server and the user's authenticator app derive the same six-digit code from a shared secret and the current time, without any network call from the app.
cards.use_when: Choosing and implementing a second factor (TOTP/hardware key) for storefront customer and admin accounts.

cards.title: WebAuthn and passkeys: replacing passwords with device-based authentication
cards.summary: WebAuthn lets users authenticate with a device-bound key or biometric (something you have/are) instead of a phishable password, using public-key cryptography so the site never receives a reusable secret.
cards.use_when: Planning a passwordless or hardware-second-factor login option for customer and admin accounts on your storefront.

cards.title: Use modern, non-guessable factors instead of knowledge-based questions
cards.summary: Classic 'something you know' factors like security questions are guessable or publicly knowable, so prefer cryptographic device factors over knowledge-based verification for recovery and sensitive actions.
cards.use_when: Designing account recovery and verification for storefront customer accounts, billing support, and admin access.

cards.title: Prevent data-breach exposure from common cloud misconfigurations
cards.summary: Breaches frequently stem from simple mistakes — publicly readable object storage, SQL injection, command injection, misconfigured servers — so audit these on your own storefront infra.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your store's storage buckets, servers, and database access for accidental public exposure.

cards.title: Audit your authentication implementation with HIBP and breach-awareness
cards.summary: Use Have I Been Pwned and similar resources to verify your own team's exposure, alert customers, and feed account-security decisions at signup and login.
cards.use_when: Standing up account-security review processes for a storefront, and checking your team's admin/ops accounts for exposure.

cards.title: Model login security as credential-to-account binding, not factors
cards.summary: Stop enumerating knowledge/possession/biometric factor categories; instead inventory every thing that can bind a customer to an account and assess each one's interception and recovery risk.
cards.use_when: Deciding what login and account-recovery methods your storefront should accept, or auditing why a 'two-factor' customer account can still be taken over.

cards.title: Attack the password-reset link as your weakest login path
cards.summary: Treat any email reset link as equivalent to a password because whoever holds the link holds the account, and harden or replace it accordingly.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing the forgot-password, magic-link login, or email-verification flow on a storefront.
